passage:
Mummy was ill for four years before she died. I was twenty-two by the end, and I knew the hospital corridors better than my college. After the funeral, the house was so quiet I couldn't sit in it. Six months later I signed up to volunteer at the hospice near our gurdwara on Saturdays. I read the newspaper aloud to patients, fetch water, hold hands when families can't come. It felt like the only useful thing I knew how to do.
Sister Nirmala, who runs the volunteers, watched me closely. Last month, after an old woman died on my shift, I went straight to the next bed. Nirmala stopped me. "Gurpreet, sit for ten minutes first. Your own grief needs a chair too."
I sat in the garden and cried for Mummy, properly, for the first time in months. I still come every Saturday. I also go to the grief group on Wednesdays now.

qa.q: Where does Gurpreet volunteer on Saturdays?
qa.a: At the hospice near the gurdwara.

qa.q: Why did volunteering feel like 'the only useful thing' to Gurpreet?
qa.a: After years of caring for Mummy, helping others gave the loss a purpose and filled the painful quiet of the house.

qa.q: What turning point showed Gurpreet that the caring work couldn't hold everything?
qa.a: Nirmala stopping Gurpreet from rushing to the next bed; sitting in the garden and crying for Mummy showed the grief needed its own space, so Gurpreet joined a grief group too.

qa.q: How might Sister Nirmala see Gurpreet's eagerness?
qa.a: She values the help but stays watchful, knowing a grieving volunteer can use the work to keep their own loss at a distance.

grounding: An adult who lost a parent to a long illness finds purpose volunteering at a hospice, and learns the grief still needs its own space.

passage:
Tutor's note, nursing school, 3 March
Francis joined our diploma course last year, eight months after his father died of kidney disease. He told the interview panel he had spent two years going to his father's dialysis sessions with him and "wanted the other families to have someone who gets it". He is one of our most careful students: gentle with elderly patients, first to volunteer for the renal ward.
This week I noticed he hasn't taken a single day off, even when unwell, and in the break room he changes the subject whenever anyone mentions fathers. When a renal patient's son thanked him on Tuesday, Francis went to the stairwell for twenty minutes.
Next step: I spoke to him today. I told him his purpose is real and valuable, and that his grief still needs its own time. He agreed to meet the college counsellor on Friday.
Ankita Rao, Clinical Tutor

qa.q: How long after his father died did Francis join the diploma course?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: Why might Francis have gone to the stairwell after the patient's son thanked him?
qa.a: The thanks probably brought his own father and the loss rushing back, feelings the busy work usually keeps at a distance.

qa.q: Which choice in Ankita's note is most helpful, and why?
qa.a: Telling Francis his purpose is valuable but his grief needs its own time, and linking him with the counsellor, so the caring work doesn't have to carry everything.

qa.q: How might the renal patients' families experience Francis?
qa.a: As someone who truly understands, gentle and careful, probably without guessing how much the work costs him.

grounding: A nursing tutor notices a student who turned his father's death into caring work avoiding his own grief, and helps him make room for it.

passage:
Sunday, late
Today was my first full shift at the daycare centre for people with memory loss. Mr D'Souza called me "Leela" all morning, and I let him. Appa used to call me by his sister's name too, near the end, and forget I was his daughter. I think that's why I'm good at this. I know how to wait while someone looks for a word. I know you don't correct, you just hold the cup steady.
Farhan, the coordinator, asked if I was sure I was ready, since it's only been ten months. I said yes, loudly. Then on the bus home a man was humming an old film song Appa loved, and I had to get off two stops early and sit on a bench.
So maybe the work isn't the whole answer. I'm keeping it. But I've told Farhan I'll take Thursdays off, and on Thursdays I'm going to go through Appa's cupboard, slowly.
Ganga

qa.q: What did Mr D'Souza call Ganga all morning?
qa.a: "Leela".

qa.q: Why does Ganga feel good at this work?
qa.a: Caring for Appa taught her to wait for words and hold the cup steady, so the loss feels like it gave her something useful to offer.

qa.q: What choice did Ganga make after the bus ride, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Keeping the work but taking Thursdays off to go through Appa's cupboard, because the grief needs its own space alongside the purpose.

qa.q: Why might Farhan have asked whether Ganga was ready?
qa.a: Farhan may have worried that starting only ten months after Appa's death, the work could stir up grief Ganga hadn't faced yet.

grounding: An adult whose father had dementia starts caring work at a memory-loss daycare and realises her grief also needs time of its own.

passage:
Joseph: how was the first week at the hospice?
Anjali: good. tiring. sat with a man called Mr Pinto for two hours today, just holding his hand
Anjali: his daughter couldn't get off work till evening. i said i'd stay
Joseph: that's a lot
Anjali: it felt right. like all those nights in Papa's ward weren't for nothing
Anjali: i know the machines, the beeps, what to say to families in the corridor. i finally know what to DO with all that
Joseph: that makes sense. can i ask something?
Anjali: ok
Joseph: when do you get to just miss him? not help anyone. just miss him
Anjali: ...
Anjali: i haven't really. not since the funeral
Anjali: every time it comes up i sign up for another shift
Joseph: the work is good. you're good at it. but maybe it can't be the only place he goes
Anjali: sunday is his birthday. maybe i'll take it off and go to church with Mummy
Joseph: want company after?
Anjali: yes. thank you

qa.q: How long did Anjali sit with Mr Pinto?
qa.a: Two hours, just holding his hand.

qa.q: Why does the hospice work feel right to Anjali?
qa.a: Anjali feels satisfied that all those nights in Papa's ward weren't for nothing; finally knowing what to do with them turns the loss into purpose.

qa.q: What choice at the end of the chat gives the grief its own space?
qa.a: Taking Sunday, Papa's birthday, off to go to church with Mummy and meeting Joseph afterwards, instead of signing up for another shift.

qa.q: What might Joseph be worried about when asking, "when do you get to just miss him?"
qa.a: Joseph seems worried that Anjali is using the work to avoid grieving, and that the sadness will stay stuck if it only ever turns into helping others.

grounding: Shows an adult who lost a parent to a long illness finding purpose in hospice work, and a friend's question reminding them that the grief itself still needs space.

passage:
In the small primary health centre at Sangamner, Vishal, twenty-four, was first to arrive and last to leave. For three years he had taken his mother by local bus to the district hospital for her treatments; since she died in March, he had enrolled as a trainee nursing assistant.
He was good at it. He knew how to lift an old farmer without hurting him, and what to say to a frightened daughter in the corridor. The senior nurse, Usha, watched him calm a whole family in five minutes.
But she also saw him flinch when a patient asked, "Your mother must be proud?" and then hurry off to restock gauze.
That evening Usha stopped him at the gate. "You're very good here, Vishal. But this place can't hold all of it. When did you last sit with your own sadness?"
He didn't answer. On Sunday, for the first time since March, he went to the temple by the river and sat there a long time, not helping anyone.

qa.q: What did Vishal enrol as after his mother died?
qa.a: A trainee nursing assistant at the small primary health centre at Sangamner.

qa.q: Why might restocking gauze feel easier to Vishal than answering the patient's question?
qa.a: The work gives his loss a purpose and keeps him busy, while the question touched the raw grief for his mother that he hadn't let himself feel.

qa.q: What turning point did Usha's question create?
qa.a: It named that the work couldn't hold all of his grief, and on Sunday he sat by the river for a long time, giving the sadness its own space.

qa.q: How does Usha see Vishal's skill with patients?
qa.a: Usha admires how well he calms families, but also notices the flinch and the constant busyness, and cares enough to say what the work can't do.

grounding: Illustrates a young man who turns the loss of his mother after a long illness into nursing work, and a senior nurse who reminds him that grief needs its own space.
